events.title: The dystopian legal architecture of the ‘war on terror’ must be dismantled
events.summary: A quarter-century after 9/11, we are still living under the security order it unleashed. Press Officer at CAGE International. A protest movement has been proscribed as a terrorist organisation, thereby criminalising support for those enduring a genocide rather than any act of violence. Migrants are being held in detention facilities modelled on the very practices documented at Guantanamo Bay, and some are even being sent to the Cuban detention camp itself. Surveillance infrastructure once built to monitor “terrorism” has quietly been turned on Palestine solidarity protesters instead. None of this sits at the edges of the law, straining against it or slipping past its limits. It sits comfortably within laws written 25 years ago, doing precisely what they were written to do. The legal architecture assembled after 9/11 was sold to the public as an emergency response to a single, unrepeatable day. A quarter of a century later, it has not been rolled back, nor even meaningfully questioned. It has simply become permanent, its reach extending steadily beyond anything its original architects would have needed to justify at the time. It is worth resisting, too, the instinct to treat 9/11 as the origin of this story. The hostility that the “war on terror” eventually gave a name to was already established Western policy long before that morning arrived; 9/11 did not invent the idea that certain populations could be treated as a security problem before they were treated as human beings; it simply furnished that idea with a name, a legal framework, and a budget without limit. Read the last 25 years as a continuation of something older, rather than an aberration that began with a single attack, and the years since start to make a different kind of sense. Seen that way, the throughline is difficult to miss. What began as indefinite detention at Guantanamo Bay has grown into the working infrastructure of a far broader security state. The same legal tools have been carried forward rather than retired, first used to justify holding men without charge, then to designate a protest movement a “terrorist” organisation for the positions it holds, and now to run immigration enforcement on a national security logic drawn directly from the “war on terror”. Each expansion has been presented, in turn, as a departure, a special case, an exception demanded by the moment. Yet this is what a permanent security architecture does once it is built: it merely shifts to its next target. The case that shows this most starkly is not one of prosecution but of detention that never required one. Mansoor Adayfi was held at Guantanamo for nearly 15 years without ever being charged with a crime, and has written of treatment no human being should have to endure. In one of the camp’s more telling episodes, he opened a boxed meal to find the words “we will never forget, we will never forgive” scrawled on the inside of the box. When he wrote back demanding justice rather than vengeance, the camp administration answered with food punishment and solitary confinement, on the grounds that his message amounted to a death threat. Guantanamo never needed a conviction to hold him for a decade and a half. It needed only the architecture built after 9/11, and the presumption embedded within it that a man like him could be treated as a suspect indefinitely, without the state ever having to prove why. What Guantanamo demonstrated, in other words, was not simply a place but a method: that indefinite suspicion could be built into law and would hold, that a population could be designated a security risk and processed accordingly, with no charge required and no real accounting demanded. It is that method, not the camp itself, that has since travelled. It is difficult to look at a proscribed protest movement or a migrant held in conditions that directly echo those at Guantanamo and not recognise the same architecture at work. The same presumption, applied differently, produced convictions elsewhere that later could not survive scrutiny: one that kept Hamid Hayat imprisoned for 14 years, secured through coerced statements, and another that kept Dr Ali al-Tamimi imprisoned or confined for 20 years, based entirely on protected speech and overturned by a US appellate court only this year. Guantanamo did not even need that pretence. It needed only the architecture itself. Twenty-five years is long enough to know that these laws were never temporary, and long enough to know they were never going to correct themselves. The only response still worth taking seriously is to abolish them. The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

events.title: The Atlantic fixed its business. Then AI came for media.
events.summary: Courtesy of The Atlantic; BI Nicholas Thompson, the CEO of The Atlantic magazine, put together a deal with OpenAI in 2024. That deal has had lots of upside for his property, he says — but delivering readers to his site is not one of them. In addition to running The Atlantic's business, Thompson also creates revenue-generating content separate from the editors and writers who work there. It's an unusual arrangement. Running a great magazine is hard. So is turning a money-losing magazine into a profit center. Nicholas Thompson has done both. The CEO of The Atlantic took the job in 2021, when it was gushing red ink and slashing its workforce. Today it's profitable, boasts 1.6 million subscribers, and revenue that Thompson says is "much bigger" than $100 million — the number it last reported in 2023. Thompson has the advantage of a very deep-pocketed owner — Laurene Powell Jobs, who is worth a reported $15 billion — and a very talented editor. Under editor in chief Jeffrey Goldberg's watch, the Atlantic has become a consistent source of must-read pieces . But Thompson is also an atypical CEO: Prior to joining The Atlantic, he had a long career as an editor at outlets like Wired and The New Yorker. On top of that, he's a prolific creator who churns out books , podcasts , and, most recently, vertical videos for a very large audience. I talked to Thompson about what it's like to work for one of the richest people in the world, what AI has done for his magazine and why it has yet to produce a breakthrough product that normal people use, and why he's a business-side executive making content that looks a lot like the stuff the editorial staff at his publication might make for themselves. You can listen to the entire interview on my Channels podcast; the following is an edited excerpt of our conversation. Peter Kafka: Like lots of publishers, The Atlantic has a billionaire owner: Laurene Powell Jobs, one of the wealthiest women in the world. What does she want from you guys, and what is she giving you? Are you supposed to be a self-sustaining business? Do you ask her for money to expand? Nicholas Thompson: My mandate when I was hired was to make it profitable. When you have wealthy owners, people don't understand that they care about taking the business seriously. You don't get to be that wealthy, and you don't maintain that wealth by not caring about how businesses are run. I think she cares a lot about improving democratic conversation in America and making sure that young people know a lot about the most important issues of the day. An ideological project. That's definitely the wrong word. I would say more like "idealistic." She cares a ton about American democracy, and she wants American democracy to work. We want to try to contribute to that. If you don't have good information, and people can't share facts, and they can't share stories, democracy is a little bit harder. Now that you're profitable, how often do you hear from her or her people? All the time. I talk to people in her office every day, and I talk to her fairly frequently. What are those conversations like? You say, "We're profitable. We probably will be more profitable next year. We're making really good work." Then what happens? You talk about things like, "What's your video strategy? Where are the best opportunities? What can you do more of? OK, is this actually working?" She's exceptionally perceptive and smart, and says, "Wait, wait a second, Nick. This thing you're doing here, is that actually really working? And is that the right person to be doing it?" Questions like that. You were one of the first publishers to sign a deal with OpenAI . [ Axel Springer , which publishes Business Insider, also has an OpenAI deal.] There was a lot of hand-wringing about that. It's been a couple of years. Has it worked the way you thought it would? I prefer them paying us than not paying us, right? And many of the AI companies don't pay. We set up a whole bunch of boundaries in the contract: How much can you summarize? Can you quote an author? Can you try to get your model to write like an author? These things we care about because we want it to be harder for AI to replace what we do. They've been great on that. We wanted to have a seat at the table as they talk through the role of journalism in their models. Absolutely. They've been amazing partners at that. The one thing that we haven't seen, and I think it's been a surprise to both parties — one reason to do the deal was my expectation that AI was going to replace traditional search, and that we wanted to make sure that there was lots of traffic directed back to us. What you hear throughout the industry is that the bots are not sending much traffic to publishers. The click-through rates are very bad. That has surprised me. Do you think that's about the way they've designed the product? If the links were bigger or more prominent, or there was some incentive to click through, you'd see the rates go up? You certainly could change it in ways that would make the rates go up. But the core problem is that people go to it for a different use case. The Google use case was people were trained to go, "I want to find this thing. Now I'll leave, and I'll click to a site." With Claude and ChatGPT, you're in a conversation with the bot. Meanwhile, Google has been sending less and less referral traffic . So I hear . Can I say something interesting about that, though? The most interesting data point to me is that the number of subscribers we get from Google traffic has gone up. Mysterious, right? What's clearly happening is that Google is sending us fewer people who aren't going to subscribe. Are they doing that deliberately? Is it because of our content mix? Is it because something in the way that we've tagged our stories? There are all kinds of different hypotheses. What would you need to re-up with OpenAI at the end of your deal? There just has to be a fair exchange of value. What are you giving us, and what are we giving you? Is it fair? And if it's not, well, then we'll block you from the site, or we'll sue you, right? That's the deal. There are lots of things they can give you of value. In the old deal, they gave us dollars, which are really nice. They [also] gave us credits, which weren't useful at the beginning, and then were incredibly useful , right? Codex credits are awesome. You make your own sponsored videos and post them on platforms like LinkedIn, where you have 1.6 million followers. You're the CEO of The Atlantic. They are not editorial products. Atlantic editor in chief Jeffrey Goldberg has nothing to do with them. Have you guys had a talk about that? The stuff the CEO makes is labeled, and it says, "This has not come from The Atlantic's editorial arm." events.title: Houthis reportedly advance to key Red Sea island, further threatening crucial oil choke point
events.summary: Iran-backed Houthis reportedly seize Yemen's Perim Island, tightening their grip on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The advance raises the risk of renewed attacks on Red Sea shipping and global trade. Iran and its proxies are now positioned to threaten key oil choke points on both sides of the Arabian Peninsula. The Iran-backed Houthis reportedly advanced to Yemen's strategic Perim Island on Friday, delivering a major boost to the militant group's push to take control of one of the world's most important shipping choke points. The capture of Perim Island, which was reported by several news agencies, citing multiple Yemeni government sources, comes just one day after the Houthis seized Yemen's port city of Mokha on the Red Sea coast. CNBC could not independently confirm the report. The rapid ground offensive is seen as a severe setback to Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni forces it backs and puts Iran and its proxies on course to exercise control over two critically important oil choke points on either side of the Arabian Peninsula: the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Strait of Hormuz . Perim Island is a small and rocky area of land that divides the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a waterway that connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and to global markets. There are concerns that the Houthis advance toward the Bab el-Mandeb Strait could have significant ramifications for global trade, particularly if the militant group ratchets up threats or attacks on Red Sea shipping. Indeed, the capture of Mokha marked a "major blow" to Saudi Arabia as it raises the possibility of the group exerting a tighter grip on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, according to Hamish Kinnear, principal Middle East and North Africa analyst at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft. Yemen's port city of Mokha is situated about 75 kilometers (46 miles) north of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. "The Houthis were already threatening Saudi shipping from previous positions, but their capture of Mocha opens up the possibility of further advances towards the Bab el-Mandeb coastline and a tighter grip on the chokepoint," Kinnear said in a research note. As the war continues, Kinnear said both Tehran and Washington believe time is on their side, making a new truce unlikely for now. "Oil and gas prices, and more specifically refined products such as diesel, will continue to tick upwards while that remains the case – even if US convoys and Strait of Hormuz export alternatives cushion the price impact," Kinnear said. The strategic importance of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has grown significantly since the start of the U.S. and Israel's war against Iran in late February , with the waterway emerging as an alternative route for crude moving toward Asia. Oil prices traded sharply lower on Friday, but both major benchmarks could still end the week above $100 per barrel for the first time since mid-May. International benchmark Brent crude futures with November expiry traded 3.3% lower at $104.21 per barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures with October expiry were last seen 3.4% lower at $99.08. The resilience of the oil market is being tested by a clearer recognition of the mounting threat to regional supply, strategists at ING said , with energy market participants seen repricing both the duration and severity of the conflict. Even as flows continue through the Strait of Hormuz, ING's strategists said flows remain well below pre-war levels, underlining how fragile the situation has become. "Saudi energy infrastructure and crude oil exports from the Red Sea are increasingly at risk, with the Houthis in Yemen targeting Saudi Arabia," ING's Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey said in a research note published Friday. "As the Houthis have taken control of the Red Sea port of Mokha in Yemen, recent events increase the threat to shipping around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait," they added.

Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta said he was “very surprised” by Gabriel Jesus’s claim that he was forced to train alone and was given no information prior to joining Barcelona. Jesus ended his four-year spell with the Gunners in September and has since made it clear he felt disappointed with the way his exit was handled. list 1 of 4 ‘Desperate’ Sabalenka targets US Open threepeat in epic Rybakina final list 2 of 4 Lights, camera, action: Irksome influencers at the US Open are here to stay list 3 of 4 Pakistan U19 cricketers mistaken for asylum seekers by protesters in UK list 4 of 4 World Athletics Ultimate Championship opens with record $10m prize pot The Brazilian striker said in an interview this week that “out of nowhere they put me to train apart from the group,” adding that “nobody told me nothing” before he signed for Barcelona. Responding to Jesus’s criticism, Arteta insisted he had spoken to the former Manchester City star about the transfer and had parted on good terms. “Very surprised, to be fair. Especially because with Gabi (Jesus) I had an individual talk in the dressing room,” he told reporters on Friday. “I don’t know what words were said; it’s fine. The words that we used were all about gratitude.” Arteta also came under fire from former Arsenal striker Ian Wright, who recently said he was “uncomfortable” with what he perceived to be a lack of dialogue between the club and Gabriel Martinelli, who moved to Saudi Pro League side Al Hilal on September 3. But Arteta used the presence of Leandro Trossard, who was sold to Besiktas in July, to watch Arsenal’s victory over Chelsea last weekend as an example of the club’s bond with their former players. “I don’t know, it’s OK. Sometimes I understand that when you have to deliver bad news, or news that people don’t expect, somebody has to be the bad cop. If I have to be, I have to be and I understand,” he said, before the Premier League champions’ trip to Sunderland on Saturday. “What is important is normally what happens three months or six months later. When Trossard comes, he’s in the dressing room with all of us, the atmosphere and the relationship you have. “Thank God so far that with all the players that left, at some point the relationship has been really good. I hope this is the same case.”

events.title: Trump dismisses AI extinction risks as more than a dozen OpenAI, Anthropic insiders call for a slowdown
events.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump said he has no concerns about AI leading to human extinction and instead emphasized staying ahead of China. Insiders at OpenAI and Anthropic have stepped up public warnings of the risks associated with developing ever more capable AI systems. Lawmakers from both parties are pursuing proposals aimed at increasing oversight of advanced AI development. U.S. President Donald Trump has dismissed warnings that AI could pose an existential threat to humanity, after a wave of insiders at frontier labs Anthropic and OpenAI stepped up public warnings of risks from the technology . When asked if he had concerns about AI leading to human extinction, Trump said, "No, I don't have any." "I have concerns that if we don't win AI, we're going to be put in a very bad position," the president told reporters Thursday. "We are leading China right now by a pretty good period, I would say a year, which is, you know, considered a lot." The U.S. and China are locked in a battle for AI supremacy, with tensions ratcheting up as Chinese AI models have become more advanced and their adoption grows across the globe. Trump's comments came after a number of researchers at frontier AI labs, including OpenAI and Anthropic, sounded the alarm over the rapid pace of development of the tech. Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon said Tuesday that he was quitting the company over concerns that Anthropic and rival OpenAI are "gambling with our lives." He added that those building AI believed that it could "kill us all by the end of the decade" — a view which has since been echoed by other employees at the labs. Many AI safety fears revolve around models developing the ability to improve their own performance, a technique known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI. "It's hard to overstate how dangerous speeding towards RSI is," said Jasmine Wang, an OpenAI researcher working on alignment, on Wednesday evening. OpenAI's chief scientist Jakub Pachocki said Saturday that he has a "strong expectation" that the speed of progress in AI could be sustained into recursive self-improvement . "I am concerned no one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence." Trump's comments come as some Republican lawmakers have joined Democrats in backing greater oversight of advanced AI systems. In July, Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., and Rep. Lori Trahan, D-Mass., announced plans to introduce a bill called the FRONTIER Act, which aims to establish a framework for governing the deployment of advanced AI models. "Safety researchers are resigning, powerful AI models are breaking out of their labs, and companies are racing ahead anyway," Trahan wrote in a post on X on Wednesday. "It's past time for Congress to get off the sidelines and do its job." Earlier this month, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, introduced a bill called the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, which would temporarily pause advanced AI development until the federal government establishes safety rules.

events.title: 'You can't break the fundamental laws of physics': T-Mobile CFO says he's not worried about Elon Musk's cellular ambitions
events.summary: Elon Musk's SpaceX has its sights set on the cellular market. T-Mobile's CFO says he's not worried. REUTERS/Steve Nesius SpaceX wants a piece of the cellphone market, but T-Mobile's CFO is far from concerned. Peter Osvaldik said "everybody in the know" is "laughing" at parts of Starlink's plans. While Starlink satellites provide coverage in remote areas, it faces different challenges in cities. Elon Musk thinks Starlink can shake up the mobile industry, but a T-Mobile exec said its strategy should be laughed out of the room. "It's not a competitive threat from a wireless perspective at all," T-Mobile CFO Peter Osvaldik said Wednesday at Citi's 2026 Global TMT Conference. "If we, as a management team, over the course of two months, changed the strategy to how we're going to roll out a wireless network like a dozen times, it would laugh us out of the room and kick me out of the management team appropriately." Musk and SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell outlined their goals for Starlink Mobile in the company's first earnings call in early August. The Big Three telecoms firms — AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile — make about $600 billion a year in revenue. "I anticipate us to be able to acquire quite a few of their customers because I think our service will be better," Shotwell said. She pointed to Starlink's ability to "eliminate dead zones" and provide coverage in remote areas through its satellites. It has 650 direct-to-cell satellites in orbit, as well as its flagship constellation of over 10,000 satellites for broadband internet. However, for urban areas, satellites aren't as useful as cell towers. Starlink's satellites operate in low Earth orbit, a few hundred miles above the planet, which means their signals reach cellphones quickly — though these signals can be blocked by typical city infrastructure. "You can't get through buildings, walls. You can't even get through a Tesla windscreen," Osvaldik said. "You can have 1 million satellites up there with all the spectrum in the world, you can't break the fundamental laws of physics." SpaceX isn't planning to rely only on satellites for Starlink Mobile . Instead of using cell towers, which are expensive and difficult to install, SpaceX wants to use a huge number of small cell stations, called femtocells. "Essentially, they're really just Starlink dishes that also provide connectivity in the mobile spectrum bands, and have them be all over the place," Musk told investors. "The Starlink antennas are located on the roofs of houses and businesses, so they've got a clear view for providing connectivity directly to cellphones on the ground." Osvaldik ridiculed this idea, saying "everybody in the know" is "laughing at" it because potentially 1 billion femtocells would be required to match the coverage of cell towers. "I mean, it's just not fathomable," he added. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Russian strikes kill two in Kyiv as Moscow targets capital’s fuel stations
events.summary: Second day of strikes on fuel stations suggest a new campaign focused on civilian areas in the Ukrainian capital. Russian drone attacks on two fuel stations in Kyiv have killed two people and injured others, as Moscow continues to target civilian areas. They were struck early on Friday within ten minutes of each other in the capital’s Obolonskyi and Dniprovskyi districts, shortly after emergency sirens rang out, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said in a statement. list 1 of 3 How Ukraine’s deepest attack in Russia, on Arctic gas, signals new reach list 2 of 3 Amnesty accuses Russia of trafficking foreigners to fight in Ukraine list 3 of 3 BRICS summit: Is the bloc truly challenging a Western-dominated world? Russia also targeted fuel stations in Kyiv on Thursday, suggesting a new campaign focused on civilian areas in the capital. Ukrainian authorities have warned people to avoid filling up when air raid sirens sound. One person died at the scene of one of the attacks, Klitschko said, while the other died in hospital. Six people required hospital treatment. While fuel stations near the eastern and southern battle lines have been hit regularly for months, authorities have long warned that the attacks could extend to the capital as an intimidation strategy. Russia and Ukraine both deny targeting civilians as the conflict – started with Moscow’s invasion in February 2022 – has developed into a series of daily attacks with missiles and drones. Other Russian drone strikes overnight hit near a shopping mall in Pavlohrad, leaving five dead and 67 injured, while a mother and son were injured in Zaporizhzhia when a drone hit an apartment building and a mall. Ukraine’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Andrii Sybiha, declared Friday a day of mourning. On Thursday, he condemned Russia for attacking civilian areas in a bid to sow fear. “Russia is systematically attacking places where it knows people will be spending their time going about their daily lives, seeking to maximise casualties, spread fear and put pressure on Ukrainian society,” he stated. Ukraine unleashed its own large-scale drone attack through the night, with Russia’s Ministry of Defence reporting that its forces shot down 777 drones in 16 regions. Two people were killed and three injured in Tula, to the south of Moscow, local authorities reported.

events.title: Activist Oasis seeks board seats at Vail Resorts
events.summary: The Scoop Activist investor Oasis Capital Management has nominated a slate of directors at Vail Resorts and is preparing to launch a proxy fight, according to people familiar with the matter. Oasis nominated former Disney CEO Bob Chapek, Ashton Hudson, Bryce Roberts, and Olympic gold medalist Picabo Street to Vail’s board, the company confirmed in a press release Friday morning . A spokesperson for Oasis did not respond to a request for comment. Semafor earlier this year reported that Oasis was likely to pursue a proxy fight and that Vail Resorts was working with advisers to help it fend off a potential activist. Know More The accelerating pace of extreme weather has made snowfall on Vail’s properties less predictable. Economic pressures have pushed consumers to pull back on spending. And Vail’s unionized workers have been fighting with management over working conditions. Looming over it all is billionaire Matthew Prince, a Park City resident who had expressed frustrations with how Vail Resorts has operated its Park City property, blaming Vail CEO Rob Katz for the company’s financial troubles . Prince did not respond to a request for comment.

events.title: ‘Key pillar’: the 5-year powerhouse plan for China’s car industry
events.summary: Beijing’s outline calls for boosting domestic market and innovation while controlling capacity to avoid involution effects China is set to secure its place among the global automotive powerhouses by 2030 through further efforts to boost domestic sales and foster technological innovation, while a capacity alert mechanism will be introduced to guard against disorderly competition. The ambitious targets and actions are laid out in the country’s 15th five-year plan for the development of the intelligent connected new-energy-vehicle industry, unveiled on Thursday by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and eight other ministries. The new-energy category comprises both battery-powered electric vehicles and plug-in hybrid models. According to the plan, China would further shore up its complete industrial supply-chain strengths in the sector and prepare for the large-scale roll-out of vehicles equipped with automated driving functions. “[By 2030] the automotive sector will solidify its standing as a key pillar of the national economy,” the plan stated. “The timing for rolling out this five-year plan is well judged,” said Cui Dongshu, secretary general of the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA). “The auto industry is undergoing structural transformation; total domestic sales are declining, as market leadership shifts from gasoline-powered passenger vehicles to electric cars.” Data from the CPCA showed around 1 million electric passenger vehicles were sold domestically in August, down 10.1 per cent from a year earlier. Total sales in the January-August period fell 12.1 per cent year on year.

events.title: Nonprofit received $2 million from Olivia Rodrigo and Melinda French Gates—it wants to give cash to abuse survivors
events.summary: Life Brides are bringing back the one-night-only bachelorette party The Next Dream The American Dream is missing a key ingredient, says expert: Without it, 'life is pretty grim' Work 26-year-old quit her corporate job to become a seamstress at Yellowstone Side Hustles NASA engineer spent $200 to start side hustle from closet—it brings in $32K/mo The Next Dream Why Gen Z doesn't see marriage as part of their American Dream At 4 p.m. on Saturday, August 29, leaders from the 10 nonprofits involved in Olivia Rodrigo's Daisy Chain Fields music festival stood, arms linked, huddled in the corner of a hangar. The group, who spent the day running booths inside the facility to introduce festival goers to their work, was told meet for an announcement, but given no other context, says FreeFrom founder and CEO Sonya Passi. Standing shoulder to shoulder, they leaned in so they could hear the news above the noise of the fans inside the hangar. Melinda French Gates was matching the $10 million proceeds raised by the event, a member of Rodrigo's team told them. That meant that FreeFrom and the other nonprofits — which included Planned Parenthood, Baby2Baby and Black Mamas Matter Alliance — would each take home $2 million, twice the amount previously announced at a press conference the day before the festival. "We were all crying," Passi, 38, says, adding: "As a founder and CEO, you're always balancing your time between raising money to do the work and doing the work. Getting that $2 million allows me to put more of my attention right now into doing the work ... and to think further ahead about building strategies that are more long-term and ultimately more effective." FreeFrom is a nonprofit working to end gender-based violence through economic interventions. The organization gives money — by way of career-building grants, a savings matching program and an emergency cash program — to survivors of abuse and advocates for statewide and federal policies that support survivors' financial security. The $2 million donation will go toward current and future initiatives, like its cash-based programs and their survivor collective, which has 600 members, Passi says. "This $2 million means that we have raised the amount of money we needed this year to break even," Passi says. Since its founding in 2016, FreeFrom has always ended each calendar year in the black, she notes, while adding: "I've had years where that moment doesn't come until the end of the year." That's the norm for many nonprofits, which often rely on donations to keep their organizations alive. Nonprofits received 37% of all 2025 online revenue in December, according to nonprofit database M+R Benchmarks ' annual report including 180 nonprofits. Rodrigo's Daisy Chain Fields Music Festival — which donated all its proceeds to nonprofits and included performances from musicians like Chappell Roan and Doechii — was modeled after Lilith Fair, a traveling music festival co-founded by singer Sarah McLachlan in 1997 that featured only female artists. Rodrigo was inspired to launch her own festival after watching girls and women connect in the crowd at her concerts, she told Rolling Stone on September 3. "I've always been so acutely aware of the power of [coming together]," she said. "And also I've always been really passionate about women's rights and reproduction healthcare, and so it just felt like a perfect thing to do." Some data shows Gen Z — Rodrigo is 23 — are likelier to participate in philanthropic causes than older generations. Over 70% of Gen Z Americans reported they "gave in some form," through donations, volunteering, fundraising or advocacy work , within the previous week, according to a 2026 survey with over 10,000 respondents conducted by GivingTuesday and GoFundMe between January 2025 and January 2026. That compares with roughly 65% of older adults who said they gave during the week prior. Passi, who became an activist at 16, founded FreeFrom a decade ago after realizing how big a role money played in survivor's independence. Three quarters of women who called the National Domestic Violence Hotline reported staying longer with a controlling partner because they were concerned about supporting themselves or children, according to survey data from over 1,800 women analyzed by Michigan State University researchers. Survivors need an average of $1,567 "to make ends meet and stay safe," but only have an average of $10 in savings and less than $300 that they can access alone, according to FreeFrom research. Passi says she was in complete shock when she heard from Rodrigo's team, who reached out to FreeFrom in June and asked if Passi would be willing to hop on a Zoom call with Rodrigo herself. "We're so lucky … I don't know how they found us, but I'm grateful they did," Passi says. At the festival, FreeFrom's booth was located in the northeast corner of the event's grounds, past a Yoko Ono-inspired wish tree and Etsy-sponsored fountain of jewelry beads.

events.title: 'Dubai will come back': ATM 2026 focuses on tourism recovery backed by events and repeat visitors
events.summary: Dubai's travel and tourism officials are cautiously optimistic about a rebound in the industry despite the Iran war, betting on Emirates airline's rapid recovery, a busy events calendar , the appeal of the city's winter season, and close collaboration between the public and private sectors. The city is preparing to host the Arabian Travel Market (ATM) from September 14 to 17 when the sector's recovery strategy will come into sharp focus against a backdrop of regional travel disruptions. Emirates recorded “quite decent” passenger demand during the summer with the airline restoring most of its pre-conflict capacity and route network, despite region-wide travel disruptions and uncertainty during the ongoing conflict, Adnan Kazim, Emirates airline's deputy president, said at a press conference ahead of ATM. The airline carried 8.7 million passengers in July and August, up from 4.7 million in March and April, he said. That is on a par with the number of passengers carried last summer, according to Emirates, which does not post monthly traffic figures. The Dubai-based carrier restored 93 per cent of its capacity and 98 per cent of its route network compared to prewar levels, according to Mr Kazim. It now flies to 140 destinations in 72 countries, with a new route to Helsinki launching on October 1. A collective focused effort on promoting Dubai as a destination that is open for business is under way to instil confidence and comfort among travellers to the emirate. “Dubai will come back and ATM will be a good milestone for that comeback to happen,” Mr Kazim said. Underpinning this recovery are Dubai's popular winter season, a busy events calendar with more than 100 exhibitions in the last four months of this year, and repeat visitors to the city including the visiting friends and relatives (VFR) segment, he said. The 33rd ATM will take place at Dubai World Trade Centre, with more than 80 destination participants and 300 host buyers. The event was postponed from its originally scheduled date in May due to the Iran war that has now entered its seventh month. The annual event will bring together tourism ministers, authorities, hotels, tour operators and exhibitors to assess the conflict's impact, rebuild traveller confidence and discuss the sector's future. Dubai attracted a record 19.6 million visitors in 2025, with highs of two million visitors in December alone, and the “trajectory is moving in the right direction”, said Issam Kazim, chief executive of Dubai Corporation for Tourism and Commerce Marketing. The current situation is affecting the number of visitors to the city because of some governments issuing travel advisories and some international airlines suspending flights, he added. Dubai is working closely with stakeholders at local and federal levels, airlines, and other partners to restore flights to the destination quickly, Mr Kazim of DCTCM said. “All the international relationships are being leveraged to ensure that … we get in as many carriers and opening flights as quickly as possible,” he said, adding that Emirates and flydubai are “plugging in the gaps” to ensure travel continues. Despite the travel advisories and some international flight suspensions, Dubai's tourism recovery plan will not be limited to regional travel, he added. “We will always obviously be optimistic about international markets as well. [Foreign visitors] are the biggest advocates of the city.” Dubai is tapping its expatriate population to help attract more international visitors and bolster its image as a safe destination open for business. It has launched a tourism incentive delivering up to Dh3,000 ($816) in discounts to residents who invite friends and family to visit the emirate. Haitham Mattar, regional director of IHG Hotels and Resorts, said it has been a “challenging time” for the tourism industry, but the sector is “way to big to fail”. “There is short-term impact on demand … however, there is continued investor confidence in markets like UAE, Saudi Arabia and Egypt,” he said. Long-term growth Dubai's tourism strategy is focused on long-term growth rather than short-term volatility. “Whether it was the financial crisis or Covid or anything else, Dubai always is looking forward,” Mr Mattar said. “We don't plan by quarters, we plan for decades ahead. “We want to make sure that as soon as things are back to normal, we're ready to pick up in a better stance and at a much stronger pace,” he added. “What better point to start than ATM itself?” 'A different ATM' Danielle Curtis, regional portfolio director at RX Global that organises ATM, said this year ATM will be “different”, but no less important. “There has been a little concern from international destinations coming in; however, our message is very clear: Dubai is open and it's business as usual,” she told The National . “It's important now more than ever for ATM to operate, to connect the industry.”

events.title: I work at Trader Joe's. I swear by these 12 purchases every time.
events.summary: As a Trader Joe's employee, I am familiar with a lot of the chain's products. However, only a few are staples in my cart each week. Heather Leith I work at Trader Joe's and regularly swear by a lot of the chain's products. In the freezer aisle, I love the fiocchetti, diner mac 'n cheese, and bulgogi beef fried rice. I also love Trader Joe's apple-cinnamon sourdough bread and non-dairy brown-sugar oat creamer. If you come through my line at Trader Joe's, you'll hear me cheerfully recommending many items — the seasonal popcorns, the newest dip, the most expensive-tasting wines under $6. However, only a few items are always in my basket during my post-shift shopping sesh. My partner and I make most meals from scratch using Trader Joe's ingredients, but I am no stranger to a microwave meal or a salad kit. For lunches and breakfasts especially, I typically mix and match items to put together a meal that requires just enough effort to make me feel like I did something. When I'm not answering questions about when the mini tote bags will be back in stock, I'm talking passionately about these — the 12 purchases I swear by. I have bought hundreds of Joe's Diner mac 'n cheese meals over the years. Heather Leith Mac and cheese is my favorite food. This frozen version beats every other store-bought mac and cheese — it even ranks higher for me than restaurant dishes. It has actual shredded cheese, so you get a nice cheese pull on every bite. I mix in a small spoonful of Trader Joe's Crunchy Chili Onion to add depth of flavor and a bit of heat. Trader Joe's sliced apple-cinnamon sourdough bread is incredible. Heather Leith This sweet sourdough with actual apple pieces was so popular this fall that Trader Joe's has made it a year-round member of the bread family. Thank goodness it's no longer a seasonal fall food , because I was suffering without it. I like to spread an ungodly amount of butter onto two freshly toasted pieces, then ascend to another planet as I eat. Pro tip from someone who often works in the bread section: Store this one on the counter to preserve its soft, chewy texture. Don't skip the cheese-filled fiocchetti with pink sauce. Heather Leith This stuffed fiocchetti pasta dish is severely underrated. I'm always recommending it to customers as they browse Trader Joe's frozen pasta section. The little bundles are filled with a ricotta cheese mix, and the pink sauce is creamy and dotted with basil. You can prepare it on the stove, but take the microwave shortcut here — it yields identical results, in my opinion. I add frozen peas to get some veggies in and tear some fresh basil on top. Trader Joe's bulgogi beef fried rice with kimchi is my perfect freezer meal. Heather Leith This savory, veggie-packed dish is filling on its own, or you can add whatever you have in your fridge to dress it up. My favorite additions are edamame, bell peppers, zucchini, spinach, tofu, Sriracha, toasted sesame seeds, and a runny fried egg on top. I pan-fry the whole situation to give the rice a golden crisp. The chicken enchiladas verde are delicious. Heather Leith If I need an easy, filling meal, I go for these flavorful chicken enchiladas in a mildly spicy green sauce. They're best when oven-baked to crisp up the edges, and I like to spoon Trader Joe's corn and chile tomato-less salsa on top. I usually eat half and have the remaining portion for lunch the next day. My favorite snack at Trader Joe's is the freeze-dried strawberry pieces. Heather Leith I am so passionate about this snack that I've had it as my official employee recommendation on an endcap display. Each bag has little bites of freeze-dried strawberries covered with a strawberry-yogurt candy coating — as a huge fan of strawberries, it's everything I want in a snack. I recently snuck a bag of these into the movie theater, and between my friends and me, it ran out before the movie even ended. Trader Joe's shredded Unexpected Cheddar goes with just about everything. Heather Leith Since I discovered these shreds, my time in the cheese aisle is much quicker. I throw a bag of this in my cart without even looking at the other options. Fans of the Unexpected Cheddar in block form know the drill — this cheddar is salty and smooth, and has a stronger aged flavor than a typical white cheddar. I add it to salads, quesadillas, and savory grain bowls. I always have Trader Joe's non-dairy oat creamer in my fridge in the brown-sugar flavor. Heather Leith I've tried every creamer Trader Joe's has, and this one is always in my fridge. It's flavorful but won't drown out the coffee taste, and the oat milk rounds out the sweetness. Nothing hits as a late-night snack like these tacos with crispy potatoes and poblano peppers. Heather Leith I like that these crispy tacos are filled with mashed potatoes and not-too-spicy poblanos. I throw them in the air fryer and dip them in Trader Joe's Guacasalsa. I regularly pick up the carrot flavor of Trader Joe's mini sheet cakes. Heather Leith Don't worry — Trader Joe's mini sheet cakes are way better than what you might expect from a grocery-store cake . The carrot-cake flavor is always moist, speckled with walnuts, and free of raisins (my ideal situation). Plus, it's topped with cream-cheese frosting. I eat a little section each night straight from the container. Trader Joe's organic fusilli corti bucati pasta is a pantry staple for me. Heather Leith Before I worked at Trader Joe's, I would buy this in bulk in case it was seasonal. Now I know it's a part of the year-round collection, but I still buy multiple bags at a time. I keep sauces pretty simple with this pasta shape, because I like the springy spirals to be the star of the bowl. They hold sauce quite nicely. I prepare the chain's BBQ-cut fresh Atlantic salmon fillets every week. Heather Leith This is my favorite cut and type of salmon anywhere, and I eat it at least once a week. The pieces are thick with just the right amount of fattiness. Each pack contains the perfect serving for one or two people. I add citrus slices and rosemary to the top, douse it in olive oil, and slow-roast it until it flakes easily with a fork. Trader Joe's was not involved in the sourcing or writing of this story. The views contained within represent the author's personal views. Keep reading our Trader Joe's diaries to see what other shoppers are putting in their carts. events.title: 25 years later, 9/11 still shapes the way we fly. Here's how air travel changed after the attacks.
events.summary: A TSA security checkpoint at John Wayne Airport in Santa Ana, California. Jeff Gritchen/MediaNews Group/Orange County Register via Getty Images Aviation security was completely overhauled after the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001. The TSA, which federalized airport security, was established in November 2001. After 9/11, only ticketed flyers were allowed past security, and cockpit doors were bulletproofed. Flying has completely changed since Al Qaeda hijackers carried out the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, 25 years ago. The newly created Transportation Security Administration replaced the private screening checkpoints that flyers were used to and introduced a new normal at airports — one where water bottles are emptied, bodies are scanned, and goodbyes are said before reaching the gate. The planes were similarly hardened with bulletproof doors and the strictest protocols for cockpit access; pilots and flight attendants also received additional training to handle terrorists. Arik Arad, who advised the President's Commission on Aviation Security and Terrorism following the 1988 bombing of Pan Am Flight 103 and served as head of security at Israel's Ben Gurion Airport , said that these changes were part of a post-9/11 paradigm shift favoring a layered approach to security. "The principle is simple — if one layer fails, another should detect or stop the threat," Arad, who now operates an aviation cybersecurity company , told Business Insider. "Intelligence, passenger assessment, screening, baggage security, airport access control, aircraft protection, trained personnel, and law enforcement all became parts of an interconnected security system. That change in philosophy was, in my view, more important than any individual technology introduced after the attacks." Here are the biggest ways flying has changed since 9/11. After the September 11 attacks, airport security was federalized through the establishment of the Transportation Security Administration. CHICAGO - SEPTEMBER 10: A security worker with the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) screens a travelers belongings September 10, 2002 in Terminal 1 at O'Hare International Airport in Chicago, Illinois. Over 500 new federally trained security workers took over the screening work today at security checkpoints in the airport's largest terminal, replacing workers from Argenbright Security. Tim Boyle/Getty Images Before 9/11, airport security was handled by numerous private companies. In November 2001, the Aviation and Transportation Security Act established the Transportation Security Administration , a federal agency whose trained workers took over security screening at airport checkpoints by November 2002. There are still 20 US airports that use private contractors instead of federal employees through the TSA's Screening Partnership Program . In an effort to curb staffing shortages and long security lines resulting from missed paychecks during government shutdowns, the Trump administration is pushing for greater privatization. The agency has also come under scrutiny for its effectiveness. In 2015, an internal Department of Homeland Security investigation found that the TSA failed to detect weapons and fake explosives carried by undercover agents 95% of the time, leading the acting head of the Transportation Security Administration to be reassigned. Cockpit doors were reinforced. 396032 01: Chief pilot of JetBlue Airways Lanny McAndrew, stands behind one of the new bullet-force-resistant cockpit doors that have been installed on all JetBlue planes after the September 11 attacks, October 17, 2001 at JFK airport in the New York borough of Queens. The reinforced cockpit doors, which cost the company approximately $10,000 per aircraft, are the first such doors to be installed on a major carrier. Spencer Platt/Getty Images Flight attendants used to have keys to open the cockpit from the outside. After 9/11, the cockpit got reinforced, bullet-resistant doors and could only be opened from the inside once locked. More air marshals were placed on flights. A federal air marshal service instructor at the TSA training center in Atlantic City, New Jersey. Rachel Wisniewski/The Washington Post via Getty Images In the years following the September 11 terrorist attacks, thousands of new air marshals were added to the Federal Air Marshal Service, which previously had fewer than 50, according to the Government Accountability Office . Pilots and flight attendants received more training in defensive tactics. ARTESIA, N.M. - OCTOBER 16: Unidentified commercial airline pilots practice defensive tactics in a Boeing 727 at the Federal Law Enforcement Training Center October 16, 2003 in Artesia, New Mexico. U.S. commmercial airline pilots take this course and others during the 56 hour, six-day Federal Flight Deck Officer training program, implemented by the TSA. Pilots are instructed in the use of firearms and other defensive tactics on board airplanes. Successful completion of the voluntary course is required before a pilot is permitted to carry a firearm onboard a commercial airplane. Jake Schoellkopf/Getty Images Mark Stephens, a retired Delta Air Lines pilot who flew for the airline for 30 years, told Business Insider that pilots were previously trained to accommodate hijackers' demands and take them where they wanted to go in order to buy time. That changed once the 9/11 terrorist attacks showed how planes themselves could be used as a weapon. "Up until September 11th, using the airplane as a kamikaze-type thing was never, ever, ever discussed," he said. After 9/11, pilots received additional defensive training focused on thwarting potential cockpit invasions and fending off attackers while seated at the controls. The Federal Flight Deck Officer program, launched in 2003, also authorized qualified pilots to carry firearms on board. More bomb-sniffing dogs were deployed to airports. WASHINGTON - DECEMBER 23: Ben (L), a member of the Transportation Security Administration Explosives Detection Canine Team, sniffs luggage under handler Corporal Deborah Myers' (L) guidance during a news conference introducing the team at Ronald Reagan National Airport December 23, 2002 in Washington, DC. Airports across the nation are coming up on the Transportation Security Administration's December 31 deadline of screening all checked luggage. Alex Wong/Getty Images Bomb-sniffing dogs had been used for security sweeps before 9/11, but the TSA took over and expanded the program in 2002, training dogs to detect explosives in and around the airport, including on persons and luggage. In 2025, the TSA's Canine Training Center deployed 1,076 transportation security specialist canine teams and traditional explosives detection canine teams at more than 100 US airports. By the end of 2002, all checked bags were screened for explosives. LOS ANGELES CA-090711- An airline bag handler helps a TSA officer as she puts luggage through X

events.title: The US Army can rush Patriot batteries off to global hot spots in days. Here's what the scramble looks like.
events.summary: The US Army can move a Patriot battery across the world in a matter of days. US Army photo The MIM-104 Patriot is a cornerstone of the Army's air defense capabilities. The Army has surged Patriot batteries across continents and around the world in response to crises. Army officers told Business Insider how Patriot crews quickly deploy into combat. The US Army's Patriot surface-to-air missile system has emerged as a cornerstone of its air defense operations in recent years, protecting American forces and allies from missile and drone threats. Getting one of the most in-demand air defense systems into position in a crisis is a massive logistical undertaking, but Army officers involved in past Patriot deployments told Business Insider that the US military can fly the crews, launchers, radars, and interceptors off to whatever hot spot needs them in just a matter of days. Deploying a Patriot battery in an emergency situation means soldiers may be sent with little warning, often with no clear sense of when they will return. These abrupt departures can be difficult for soldiers and their families. "Ultimately, we're first responders," said Capt. Morgan Lloyd, a Patriot battery commander. "We needed to go, so we went," he said of a past deployment. "Soldiers were proud to do it." The first 48 hours after orders are given The Army has repeatedly had to surge Patriot batteries into hot spots in response to global crises in recent years, including Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the various conflicts in the Middle East . Deployments have differed in destination, but the Army officers Business Insider spoke with said the process was remarkably similar in execution. The calls came with little warning, triggering a scramble. Days later, though, the Patriots were in position, ready to defend the skies against airborne threats — everything from crewed planes to missiles to drones. The US has deployed Patriot batteries to Eastern Europe and the Middle East in recent years. US Army photo Lloyd recalled a deployment in support of Middle East operations. He was stationed in Germany when the call came in on a Wednesday evening informing him that he needed to head out. That started the clock on a 48-hour rush to determine who was going — he could take just 80 soldiers and only the equipment that was absolutely necessary — and then get them through deployment processing and aboard a Boeing C-17 Globemaster III transport plane that would take them where they were needed. During those first two days, soldiers completed medical, legal, and administrative readiness procedures, including sorting wills, life insurance, official photos, and last-minute health checks to ensure they could deploy. At the battalion headquarters, commanders connected with host countries so political leaders knew the Army was coming. Meanwhile, troops and equipment went through final checks. The same rapid sequence plays out across Patriot deployments. "The next thing you know, you just see streams of C-17s coming in — just flooding in — loading equipment," said Lt. Col. C.S. Craig, a Patriot battalion commander, who shared details of a 2022 deployment after Russia's invasion. That deployment, he said, saw roughly 20 C-17s fly around the clock between Germany and Poland to move the soldiers needed for half a battalion, or two batteries. A Patriot battery typically consists of six mobile launch vehicles that fire interceptors, such as the popular PAC-3 missile , along with radars, a command-and-control suite, and various support equipment to sustain operations. Craig called the C-17 flight the "fun part" for soldiers. He said that the feeling of being crammed into the plane, loaded with heavy equipment held down by chains, is like having "game-day butterflies in your stomach." The Army relies on C-17 transport aircraft to move the Patriot batteries. US Air Force photo "It's exhilarating, and it's exciting," he said, "but it's also a little bit daunting." A burden for soldiers and families Before soldiers deploy, there is often a sense of uncertainty. For his deployment, Lloyd recalled, there was no set mission end date. The instructions his battery received were simple: "This needs to be defended; go out there now." This quickly posed a logistical challenge. Since the mission duration was unclear, Lloyd had to ensure that the soldiers he selected had enough time before they returned to the US for their next assignment. And that was just one consideration of many. The broader uncertainty and the understanding that air defense is a dangerous undertaking aren't felt only by the soldiers. "On the families, it's hard," Lloyd said. "I had a six-month-old son at home — didn't know if or when I'd see him again." He said that saying goodbye to his family was emotional. He recalled how two soldiers had leave approved so they could get engaged. "They had the rings, and they told me about their plans and were all excited. And of course, that got put on pause," Lloyd said. Patriot battery deployments are full of uncertainty, including mission duration. US Army photo There is a brief ceremony before troops deploy. Craig, who oversaw one such send-off, told Business Insider about talking with the soldiers and their families. "I'm telling them: 'Your loved ones are leaving. I can't tell you where they're going, and I don't know when they're going to come back.' And that's tough," he said. 'A lot of this is without sleep' When Patriot batteries deploy in a crisis, the process sometimes occurs so fast that the soldiers don't know exactly where their C-17s will land within a host country. This forces soldiers and their commanders to solve problems on the fly. "We moved so fast in Poland that we didn't have anywhere to go," Craig said, adding that the Army arrived at an airfield with many details still to be figured out. He said sometimes, "we're moving faster than the political levels can catch up," reflecting the urgency behind some of these snap deployments. "It's a complex operation that has a lot of moving parts," he said. For Lloyd's deployment, his battery received its orders on a Wednesday night, and by Saturday afternoon, the first C-17 was on the ground in the host country. The system's launchers were ready for action by Monday. From first notification, "to the time you're ready to put birds in the air, you're looking at about 96 to 120 hours. And a lot of this is without sleep," Craig said. Soldiers and commanders sometimes have to solve problems on the fly. US Army photo Lloyd said the constant communication with higher headquarters throughout the process made it feel "like the moon landing." Then came the waiting. Between maintaining the Patriot systems and monitoring intelligence for signs of an incoming attack, crews fill the downtime with books, card games, board games like Monopoly, and video games on devices like the Nintendo Switch. events.title: Next growth in the spotlight after shrugging off high street pressures
events.summary: Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in Last month, Next upgraded its profit guidance for the second time this financial year. For free real time breaking news alerts sent straight to your inbox sign up to our breaking news emails I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice Investors will be hoping Next can point towards continued sales growth after positive recent updates by the retail giant. Experts have said expectations will be “sky-high” for the group’s half-year results on Thursday September 17 after over-delivering in recent updates. Last month, Next upgraded its profit guidance for the second time this financial year after revealing sales were stronger than expected in the second quarter. It had revealed a surge in sales linked to hot weather and the release of pent-up demand in the Middle East. The fashion and homeware retailer is expected to confirm next week that total full-price sales, which excludes discounts and clearance items, increased by 9.2% over the 13 weeks to August 1, compared with the same period last year. The company improved its sales guidance in August after previously indicating sales were likely to rise by around 4% in the quarter. As a result, it is set to confirm that sales grew by around 7.7% over the first half of the year. It is predicting full-price sales growth of around 6.3% for the year and a pre-tax profit of around £1.24 billion for the year. However, investors will be hopeful that positive momentum will allow the company to deliver another improvement in its guidance next week. Richard Hunter, head of markets at Interactive Investor, said: “Expectations will, as ever, be sky-high for Next, whose tendency to under-promise and over-deliver has led to an almost guaranteed profit upgrade, while leaving analysts scratching for new superlatives. “The group’s second quarter update was no exception, with Next breezing past its own estimates and raising its profit guidance for the year as a whole.” Aarin Chiekrie, equity analyst at Hargreaves Lansdown , said: “That outlook may prove overly cautious, given Next’s core middle-aged and middle-income customers are proving relatively resilient in the current economic climate. “As a result, further small guidance upgrades over the second half can’t be ruled out.” But Next, which also owns brands including FatFace, Cath Kidston and Made.com, is still expected to report a dip in sales from its stores for the year so far, as high street footfall comes under pressure on cautious sentiment among shoppers. events.title: UK chancellor urged to remove ‘hidden taxes’ from energy bills
events.summary: Businesses, charities and other groups sign letter calling for levies to be paid by the government More than 120 organisations including big businesses and charities have called for the removal of “hidden taxes” added to energy bills to help reduce costs for consumers and prevent businesses closing. In a letter to the chancellor the signatories – including Energy UK, business trade body the CBI, End Fuel Poverty and Age UK – called for levies amounting to 10% of energy bills that fund policies to be paid for by the government. John Healey is to present his first budget on 28 October. The signatories want the remainder of the levy funding the building of renewable energy projects to be scrapped. The former chancellor, Rachel Reeves, shifted 75% of the funding to government taxation last year. The organisations also called for an end to levies to help build nuclear power plants, the funding of the warm homes discount scheme and the feed-in tariff programme, which was closed in 2019 but continues to pay businesses and customers with ongoing contracts for generating their own energy and supplying excess back into the grid. The letter argues that moving levies off bills would lower the total average household bill by as much as £250 a year, including the £150 saving from Reeves’s moves to cut some levies funding green energy schemes , and lower electricity prices for businesses by 20%. “The UK is actively sabotaging its own efforts to bring down energy costs by taxing electricity,” said Ed Matthew, director of UK programme at thinktank E3G, which co-authored the letter alongside Energy UK. “Any credible plan to tackle the cost of living and enable reindustrialisation needs to include removing these taxes from bills to the exchequer.” Last year, Britain’s biggest energy supplier, Octopus, said bills were on track to increase by 20% over the next four years , even if wholesale prices were to drop, because of the increasing amount levied due to the rising cost of government policies. The outbreak of the Iran war has pushed gas and electricity prices up with households facing the highest energy charges in three years this winter. The energy consultant Cornwall Insight forecast that Ofgem, the UK regulator, will increase its quarterly price cap again in January, putting the average annual bill at £1,872. The government faces growing pressure to tackle the UK’s energy costs, which are some of the highest in the developed world, after its pre-election promise in 2024 to cut energy bills by £300 a year by 2030. The letter , which has been backed by 123 organisations, including energy companies, business bodies, banks, retailers and campaigning groups, says UK energy bills are 70% higher now than they were in 2021. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning In July, Andy Burnham announced a cut to VAT on domestic energy bills from October , an average saving of £45, although this reduction is currently set to stay in place only until April. “High electricity prices hurt all of us,” said Dhara Vyas, chief executive of Energy UK. “By taking levies off the bill, the government can show it is serious about tackling fuel poverty and the cost-of-living crisis, growing the economy, and bringing down inflation. Cheaper electricity would have an outsized impact across the economy.” The letter also warned of the impact on companies, saying: “High energy costs are widely recognised as a significant constraint across the economy, driving business closures and job losses, while simultaneously deterring investment in the UK.”

events.title: Why the Trump administration’s bid to end diversity efforts at nonprofit schools is likely to get tied up in court
events.summary: Some 18,000 private schools could be affected by a proposed new rule if it goes into effect. Jumping Rocks/Universal Images Group via Getty Images The Trump administration wants to strip all nonprofit colleges, universities and private K-12 schools of their tax-exempt status if any of their programs designed to help students uses race as a criterion for eligibility. This change is included in a rule the Treasury Department and Internal Revenue Service proposed on Sept. 3, 2026 . The rule could take effect after May 31, 2027, following a two-month-long comment period – as long as it’s not blocked or delayed by the legal challenges likely to arise. As a nonprofit law scholar who helps nonprofit leaders understand the legal issues they face , I believe this latest salvo in the Trump administration’s attempt to end racial preferences stretches U.S. law so far that it will likely be tied up in court for years. What is the Trump administration aiming to do? The proposed rule states that private schools aren’t eligible for tax-exempt status if they have any school-administered or -supported program that “discriminates on the basis of race, color, or national or ethnic origin … for any purpose.” The regulations do not define the word “discriminate” in this context, but Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has made clear that the Trump administration considers programs that have diversity goals to be a form of discrimination. Private K-12 schools, colleges, universities and professional and trade schools would be subject to this rule, including all academic and athletic programs as well as all scholarships and admissions policies having anything to do with efforts to increase diversity. The proposed rule would not apply to religious schools that make admitting people who adhere to the school’s religion a priority. Nor would it apply to public universities, but I believe the language is broad enough to apply to the foundations that provide scholarships to students at public universities. At this point, many key details about the rule remain unclear. A group of graduates takes part in the Black Commencement at Harvard University on May 23, 2017. Keith Bedford/The Boston Globe via Getty Images The IRS estimates that this rule would affect 18,000 private schools attended by 750,000 students at all levels of instruction. All private schools that are nonprofits depend on this tax exemption, both to save money on income and property tax bills and to attract donations . Without these benefits in place, tuition bills at nonprofit schools could skyrocket and the financial pressures many colleges and universities already face would increase. Americans gave about US$92 billion in charitable donations to private schools in 2025, which mostly supported higher education. That funding covers an average of about 10% of college and university budgets . A change in the rules could also complicate schools’ relationships with their donors, alter the distribution of scholarships and lead to significant legal bills, as the government itself has acknowledged . What rationale has the administration provided? The proposed rule hinges on the Trump administration’s definition of racial discrimination: that any kind of racial preference is wrong and grounds for terminating government support – even when it’s meant to address past injustices, like the decades of systemic discrimination that followed the end of slavery in the United States. The IRS’ explanation of this rule alludes to many legal precedents, including two significant U.S. Supreme Court decisions. With its Bob Jones University v. United States ruling, the court found in 1983 that a university banning interracial dating and marriage provided the IRS with the legal grounds to revoke its tax-exempt status . And the court found in 2023, in its Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard ruling, that colleges and universities that accept government funding cannot consider race in their admissions policies without violating the equal protection clause of the Constitution. Does the federal government have this authority? There is evidence that the government lacks the authority to implement this proposed rule. Educational groups, such as EdTrust and the American Association of University Professors , have expressed their opposition to the proposed changes. Legal scholars, such as Philip Hackney, Ellen Aprill, Daryll Jones and Brian Galle , have explained why the rule is likely illegal. Two courts found on June 30, 2026, that the Department of Education did not have the authority to alter student loan forgiveness rules for the employees of nonprofits . I expect to see opponents of the proposed rule to use those cases to support this argument. Even if the courts determine the IRS does have authority to issue this rule, they will have the final say as to whether the agency has interpreted congressional intent correctly. Legal scholars are also saying that the Trump administration’s interpretation of prior Supreme Court cases regarding discrimination at schools with tax-exempt status is incorrect. They point out that the Harvard admissions case was limited to colleges and universities that accepted public funding, and it provided some narrow exceptions. The proposed regulation would apply to all private schools, without exception, even if they don’t receive federal funding. Further, the Bob Jones ruling stressed that a nonprofit’s tax-exempt status could only be revoked on “fundamental public policy” grounds when the activity in question so shocked the community conscience that it undermined any other benefit the institution conferred. It based its opinion on 30 years of evidence from all three branches of government to show that this kind of prejudice violated fundamental public policy. The Trump administration may be unable to show that the public’s perspective regarding diversity, equity and inclusion has changed that much. It faces numerous lawsuits challenging its definition of racial discrimination, and the American public remains overwhelmingly in favor of diversity, equity and inclusion policies. Law professor Roger Colinvaux has also pointed out that interpreting the term “discrimination” to mean that organizations can no longer remedy past discrimination runs counter to the legal definition of the term “charitable,” which means to help those in need. Treasury Department regulations define charitable activities as helping “the poor and disadvantaged” and eliminating “prejudice and discrimination.” Finally, as Alexander Reid, a prominent attorney who specializes in tax exemptions, noted in a letter to the IRS , the proposed rule raises significant First Amendment issues of freedom of speech , religion, association and institutional autonomy. That’s because it would affect choices that all private schools make that are essential to their identities and expression of ideas. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is pushing for the new rule.
