events.title: OpenAI's historic math solution overshadowed by credit controversy
events.summary: OpenAI says its AI has solved the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize problem, a potentially historic breakthrough shadowed by questions over unpublished research by outside mathematicians. Why it matters: The controversy strikes at a core trust question for AI-assisted science: whether researchers can safely use frontier labs' tools to work on unpublished discoveries. State of play: OpenAI said Tuesday an internal model "significantly more capable than GPT-6 Astra" produced a proof that the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations can develop a singularity in finite time. The company says the effort began Sept. 1, after OpenAI researchers heard rumors that two Millennium Prize problems had been solved and launched its new internal model at the remaining problems. On a call with reporters, OpenAI executives said they devoted enormous computing power to the effort, putting the cost of solving the problem in the "millions of dollars" with roughly 10,000 agents at work. The equations help explain how fluids move, which could be used to better understand everything from blood circulation to weather patterns. Friction point: NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster and Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge had been working on closely related fluid-dynamics research. Buckmaster publicly questioned whether OpenAI raced down a research direction it learned about from their work and raised concerns about whether private Codex material could have played a role. He also alleged that OpenAI researcher Sébastien Bubeck pushed to remove Alpöge from authorship because he works for Anthropic, OpenAI's biggest competitor. Buckmaster said that when he threatened to make their interactions public, Bubeck allegedly responded: "Why would you ruin your career?" Between the lines: The controversy raises thorny questions about who owns the work completed with AI tools, and whether the labs are competing with their own customers. Zoom in: OpenAI says it did not access Buckmaster or Alpöge's specific user data while pursuing the proof. But the company acknowledged Tuesday that it can't entirely rule out an indirect connection. "While unlikely, we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models," OpenAI said. By default, OpenAI says it doesn't train on inputs or outputs from enterprise customers. Users of personal ChatGPT accounts can opt out of having their conversations used for training. What they're saying: "Now that we can see their work, the approaches appear to be different," OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wrote on X. Altman admitted OpenAI launched the effort after hearing rumors that Anthropic's models had solved a major math problem: "We were curious if ours could do it too." OpenAI says it does not intend to claim the $1 million Millennium Prize, instead framing the result as evidence of how quickly its most advanced systems are improving. Mady's thought bubble: It's striking that OpenAI spent millions of dollars in compute chasing a math breakthrough after hearing that outside researchers — including an Anthropic employee — were close to one themselves. The episode raises an uncomfortable question: What happens when the company providing scientists with AI research tools can also mobilize vastly more resources to compete with them? The bottom line: Disputes over what AI companies know about your work and usage of their tools are just beginning.

events.title: Saudi wealth fund takes its capital pitch to Wall Street
events.summary: The Scoop Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund is set to meet some of Wall Street’s biggest firms in New York this week as it seeks foreign backing for its spending plans amid cash constraints at home. Public Investment Fund’s senior management — along with representatives of some of its biggest companies including AI firm HUMAIN, Riyadh’s King Abdullah Financial District, and luxury hotel developer Red Sea Global — will be in New York later this week, according to people familiar with the matter. They are expected to meet with investors including Apollo, Blackstone, Brookfield, Carlyle, KKR, and Stonepeak, as well as the US Export-Import Bank. The Saudi delegation is not fundraising for a specific project from the event, which is being arranged by US investment bank Lazard. The meetings are intended to familiarize investors with PIF and its portfolio, laying the groundwork for future debt or equity fundraising from global investors, the people said. PIF is ramping up efforts to attract foreign investors as it looks to reduce its reliance on direct funding and bring greater external scrutiny of its plans. The nearly $1 trillion fund, chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman, has spent hundreds of billions of dollars over the past decade creating companies and developing real estate projects. That spending was supposed to catalyze foreign investment into the kingdom, but so far the results have been short of Saudi expectations: the country attracted $32.6 billion in net inflows last year, still far from its target of $100 billion in FDI by 2030. Lazard declined to comment. PIF didn’t respond to requests for comment. Know More PIF’s latest five-year plan , unveiled earlier this year, emphasizes spending discipline, value realization from its portfolio, and attracting third-party capital. It said its 2026-2030 plan will be “underpinned by increasingly diversified financial returns, greater private sector and capital markets participation in Saudi Arabia, and continued operational and institutional excellence.” Reducing PIF subsidiaries’ dependence on state finances has long been part of the fund’s strategy. Weaning units off of state coffers has become more urgent given the slow uptick of FDI and runaway spending or over ambitious plans at several PIF companies. Some of PIF’s most high-profile bets have been dramatically scaled back as a result. PIF pulled funding for the new golf tournament LIV Golf after it poured around $5 billion into the venture with no return. NEOM, the vast real estate project on the kingdom’s west coast, has also been sharply scaled back after spending $64 billion with little to show for it. Other investments have made more progress. HUMAIN has signed partnerships with several US tech firms and says it is already attracting external financing for its data centers, while Red Sea Global has opened several luxury tourist resorts on the kingdom’s west coast and plans to expand to other markets. Notable PIF is preparing to make a more aggressive push to sell mature assets, pursue listings and divestments, and finance more of its operations and investments with external capital, Bloomberg reported in August .

events.title: Republican exploits divided field in Montana Senate race
events.summary: The failure of two candidates — one Democratic and one independent — to consolidate anti-Republican support against GOP candidate Kurt Alme is propelling him to victory, according to polling first shared with Semafor. Alme is currently winning 44% of the vote, while independent Seth Bodnar is capturing 22% and Democrat Alani Bankhead is getting 19%, according to a late August survey from Peak Insights commissioned by the Alme campaign. Thirteen percent of voters remain undecided. Both Bodnar and Bankhead declined to withdraw from the race this summer as they split the anti-Alme vote, a dynamic that has cleared the path for Alme to succeed retiring Sen. Steve Daines, R-Mont. The poll finds that Bodnar and Bankhead are splitting the Democratic vote, 49% to 43% respectively. Bodnar is only narrowly winning independent voters over Alme.

events.title: NYC unveils records suggesting officials knew air was unsafe after 9/11
events.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani 's administration released more than 170,000 pages of documents Tuesday that suggest city officials knew air conditions following the 9/11 attacks were unsafe, despite assurances otherwise. The big picture: Twenty-five years later, New Yorkers are still seeking a full accounting of what city officials knew about the toxic air around Ground Zero and whether they were honest with the public about the risks. More New York City Fire Department members have died of 9/11-related illnesses than the 343 killed in the attacks. "It would be one thing if government had stood alongside survivors and provided them with everything they needed at every step of the way, and yet we know that could not be further from what actually happened," Mamdani said during Tuesday remarks. "People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air." Driving the news: The release includes air quality reports, contamination records and internal correspondence that shed light on what city officials knew about the toxic air near Ground Zero. The public portal where the memos are stored was a more than $34 million commitment from City Hall, Mamdani said. The released followed a settlement struck between Mamdani's administration and advocacy group 9/11 Health Watch, which has waged a long fight for transparency. 9/11 Health Watch executive director Ben Chevat said Tuesday that "since 9/11, four different mayoral administrations worked to keep the answer from the public, even as city officials at the time continued to say that the air was quote 'safe and acceptable.'" The portal hosts what was found in 68 boxes of toxin-related documents uncovered by City Hall officials last year and archives from former Mayor Rudy Giuliani's office, like the so-called Harding Memo that predicted lawsuits related to toxic exposure, among other records. Mamdani said that the city would continue to update the portal and, as part of the settlement, would appoint designated personnel to coordinate document gathering to help individuals obtain victim health benefits. Since its 2011 reopening, the federally funded 9/11 Victim Compensation Fund has awarded more than $16.8 billion to over 71,000 claimants, per its most recent annual report . Flashback : Christine Todd Whitman, the former head of the Environmental Protection Agency under the Bush administration, told The Guardian 10 years ago that she was wrong to assure New Yorkers that the air was safe. What they're saying: Comedian Jon Stewart, who in the years following the attack became a vocal advocate for first responders' health, said at Tuesday's announcement that the city "buried" evidence for 25 years, starting soon after the attacks. He put it bluntly: "The city began covering their ass three weeks in." Go deeper: Accused 9/11 plotters to stand trial in 2028
